papers.core_contribution: Introduces query circuit discovery for local, input-level explanations of LLMs, proposes a robust evaluation metric (NDF) and sampling-based methods (BoN) to efficiently identify sparse, faithful circuits.
papers.conclusion: Query circuit discovery, aided by BoN sampling and NDF, demonstrates that compact sub-networks can explain much of an LLM's behavior on individual queries, offering a promising path for scalable, faithful explanations of LLM decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Extremely sparse query circuits (e.g., 1.3% of edges) can recover a large portion (e.g., 60%) of model performance on individual queries.
Best-of-N (BoN) sampling effectively discovers faithful query circuits, outperforming baseline methods.
Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF) is a more robust evaluation metric for query circuits compared to Normalized Faithfulness Score (NFS).
Query circuits enable local, prompt-level explanations of LLM decisions, offering a step towards scalable interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The method neglects combinatorial interactions among edges, which is a fundamental limitation of using indirect effects as edge scores.
The work focuses on queries with single-token outputs (e.g., option IDs) and does not address multi-token generations.
There is no automated method for interpreting the functionalities of identified edges and nodes; manual investigation is not scalable.
future_direction: Develop methods to account for combinatorial interactions among edges in circuit discovery.
Extend query circuit discovery to multi-token generations.
Integrate automated interpretability methods to explain the functionalities of discovered circuits.
papers.abstract: Explaining why a language model produces a particular output requires local, input-level explanations. Existing methods uncover global capability circuits (e.g., indirect object identification), but not why the model answers a specific input query in a particular way. We introduce query circuits, which directly trace the information flow inside a model that maps a specific input to the output. Unlike surrogate-based approaches (e.g., sparse autoencoders), query circuits are identified within the model itself, resulting in more faithful and computationally accessible explanations. To make query circuits practical, we address two challenges. First, we introduce Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF), a robust metric to evaluate how well a discovered circuit recovers the model's decision for a specific input, and is broadly applicable to circuit discovery beyond our setting. Second, we develop sampling-based methods to efficiently identify circuits that are sparse yet faithfully describe the model's behavior. Across benchmarks (IOI, arithmetic, MMLU, and ARC), we find that there exist extremely sparse query circuits within the model that can recover much of its performance on single queries. For example, a circuit covering only 1.3% of model connections can recover about 60% of performance on an MMLU questions. Overall, query circuits provide a step towards faithful, scalable explanations of how language models process individual inputs.

papers.title: From Sparse Dependence to Sparse Attention: Unveiling How Chain-of-Thought Enhances Transformer Sample Efficiency
papers.research_question: How does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) improve the sample efficiency of transformers in learning parity functions, and does it do so by introducing sparse sequential dependencies that lead to sparse attention patterns?
papers.core_contribution: CoT improves sample efficiency by introducing sparse sequential dependencies in the data, which transformers learn to capture with sparse and interpretable attention patterns, enabling polynomial sample complexity instead of exponential.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-Thought enhances transformer sample efficiency by creating sparse sequential dependencies that are efficiently captured through sparse attention patterns, leading to polynomial sample complexity for learning parity functions.
papers.key_findings:
Without CoT, learning parity functions requires exponentially many samples in the hardness parameter k, while with CoT, it requires only polynomial samples.
CoT introduces sparse sequential dependencies among input tokens, which transformers learn to represent with sparse attention patterns.
The sparsity of attention layers, measured by normalized attention entropy, is crucial for the sample efficiency improvement induced by CoT.
Multi-pass training without CoT can also lead to sparse attention and learning, but is significantly less efficient than training with CoT.
Real-world CoT data (GSM8K) induces sparser attention patterns in pretrained language models compared to non-CoT data.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex tasks and architectures
Exploring how sparsity can be leveraged to design more efficient training methods
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) significantly enhances the reasoning performance of large language models (LLM). While current theoretical studies often attribute this improvement to increased expressiveness and computational capacity, we argue that expressiveness is not the primary limitation in the LLM regime, as current large models will fail on simple tasks. Using a parity-learning setup, we demonstrate that CoT can substantially improve sample efficiency even when the representation power is sufficient. Specifically, with CoT, a transformer can learn the function within polynomial samples, whereas without CoT, the required sample size is exponential. Additionally, we show that CoT simplifies the learning process by introducing sparse sequential dependencies among input tokens, and leads to a sparse and interpretable attention. We validate our theoretical analysis with both synthetic and real-world experiments, confirming that sparsity in attention layers is a key factor of the improvement induced by CoT.

papers.title: Towards Interpretable Sequence Continuation: Analyzing Shared Circuits in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether large language models re-use circuits across analogous tasks that share common abstractions, specifically for sequence continuation tasks, and how these shared circuits function.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers shared sub-circuits in GPT-2 Small and Llama-2-7B that are responsible for sequence member detection and next member prediction across similar sequence continuation tasks, revealing that semantically related tasks rely on shared circuit subgraphs with analogous roles.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies shared sub-circuits across similar sequence continuation tasks, advancing the understanding of how transformers leverage shared computations for analogous tasks, which is a step towards more interpretable and aligned models.
papers.key_findings:
Shared sub-circuits exist for similar sequence continuation tasks (numerals, number words, months) in GPT-2 Small.
The shared sub-circuit includes attention heads with specific functionalities: sequence member detection heads (e.g., 1.5, 4.4) and successor heads (e.g., 9.1).
Analogous sub-circuits are found in Llama-2-7B with similar functionalities (e.g., attention head 5.25 as sequence detection, 20.17 as successor head).
Ablating these sequence continuation components affects performance on math-related prompts like intervaled sequences and arithmetic.
The model uses MLP 9 as a key component for predicting the next sequence member.
future_direction: Future studies can examine if this appears in even more models.

Future work can expand upon these studies by understanding how non-linear features causally effect other parts of a neural network, and possibly steer groups of non-linear features to observe their downstream effects on math-related circuits.

papers.title: Efficient Automated Circuit Discovery in Transformers using Contextual Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and accurately discover circuits (computational subgraphs) in transformers for mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces contextual decomposition for transformers (CD-T), a mathematical method for efficient automated circuit discovery that significantly reduces runtime and recovers manual circuits with high accuracy.
papers.conclusion: CD-T is a promising method for efficient automated mechanistic interpretability, paving the way for new insights into the workings of large language models.
papers.key_findings:
CD-T reduces circuit discovery runtime from hours to seconds compared to ACDC and EAP.
CD-T recovers manual circuits with an average of 97% ROC AUC on three standard tasks (IOI, Greater-than, Docstring).
CD-T circuits are 80% more faithful than random circuits of up to 60% of the original model size.
CD-T circuits can perfectly replicate original model behavior (faithfulness=1) using fewer nodes than baselines.
CD-T is the first method to efficiently produce circuits as fine-grained as attention heads at specific sequence positions.
papers.abstract: Automated mechanistic interpretation research has attracted great interest due to its potential to scale explanations of neural network internals to large models. Existing automated circuit discovery work relies on activation patching or its approximations to identify subgraphs in models for specific tasks (circuits). They often suffer from slow runtime, approximation errors, and specific requirements of metrics, such as non-zero gradients. In this work, we introduce contextual decomposition for transformers (CD-T) to build interpretable circuits in large language models. CD-T can produce circuits of arbitrary level of abstraction, and is the first able to produce circuits as fine-grained as attention heads at specific sequence positions efficiently. CD-T consists of a set of mathematical equations to isolate contribution of model features. Through recursively computing contribution of all nodes in a computational graph of a model using CD-T followed by pruning, we are able to reduce circuit discovery runtime from hours to seconds compared to state-of-the-art baselines. On three standard circuit evaluation datasets (indirect object identification, greater-than comparisons, and docstring completion), we demonstrate that CD-T outperforms ACDC and EAP by better recovering the manual circuits with an average of 97% ROC AUC under low runtimes. In addition, we provide evidence that faithfulness of CD-T circuits is not due to random chance by showing our circuits are 80% more faithful than random circuits of up to 60% of the original model size. Finally, we show CD-T circuits are able to perfectly replicate original models' behavior (faithfulness $ = 1$) using fewer nodes than the baselines for all tasks. Our results underscore the great promise of CD-T for efficient automated mechanistic interpretability, paving the way for new insights into the workings of large language models.

papers.title: Verifying Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Its Computational Graph
papers.research_question: Does the computational graph of Chain-of-Thought reasoning steps contain structural fingerprints that distinguish correct from incorrect steps?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Circuit-based Reasoning Verification (CRV), a white-box method that uses structural fingerprints from attribution graphs to verify and correct Chain-of-Thought reasoning errors.
papers.conclusion: By analyzing the computational process of LLMs, CRV enables a deeper, causal understanding of reasoning failures, moving beyond simple error detection.
papers.key_findings:
Structural signatures of error in attribution graphs are highly predictive of reasoning correctness.
These signatures are domain-specific, with distinct computational patterns for different reasoning tasks.
The signatures are causal; targeted interventions on transcoder features can correct faulty reasoning.
CRV outperforms black-box and gray-box baselines in verification accuracy.
Error fingerprints are task-specific but can be combined in a multi-task classifier.
papers.limitation:
Computational intensity of CRV makes it impractical for real-time verification.
Aggregative feature analysis does not fully exploit semantic content of individual transcoder features.
Generalizability of error signatures across different model architectures and scales is unproven.
Fidelity of interpretability tools (transcoders, attribution methods) limits analysis resolution.
future_direction: Developing more sophisticated classifiers that operate on the semantics of transcoder features.
Studying generalizability of error signatures across model paradigms and scales.
Improving fidelity of interpretability tools for more precise analysis.
papers.abstract: Current Chain-of-Thought (CoT) verification methods predict reasoning correctness based on outputs (black-box) or activations (gray-box), but offer limited insight into why a computation fails. We introduce a white-box method: Circuit-based Reasoning Verification (CRV). We hypothesize that attribution graphs of correct CoT steps, viewed as execution traces of the model's latent reasoning circuits, possess distinct structural fingerprints from those of incorrect steps. By training a classifier on structural features of these graphs, we show that these traces contain a powerful signal of reasoning errors. Our white-box approach yields novel scientific insights unattainable by other methods. (1) We demonstrate that structural signatures of error are highly predictive, establishing the viability of verifying reasoning directly via its computational graph. (2) We find these signatures to be highly domain-specific, revealing that failures in different reasoning tasks manifest as distinct computational patterns. (3) We provide evidence that these signatures are not merely correlational; by using our analysis to guide targeted interventions on individual transcoder features, we successfully correct the model's faulty reasoning. Our work shows that, by scrutinizing a model's computational process, we can move from simple error detection to a deeper, causal understanding of LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Comprehension Without Competence: Architectural Limits of LLMs in Symbolic Computation and Reasoning
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models (LLMs) systematically fail at tasks requiring symbolic reasoning, arithmetic accuracy, and logical consistency, despite being able to fluently explain the correct principles?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes a fundamental architectural limitation in LLMs termed the 'computational split-brain syndrome,' where models can explain principles they cannot reliably execute, due to geometric separation of instruction and execution pathways.
papers.conclusion: LLMs function as powerful pattern completion engines but lack the architectural scaffolding for principled, compositional reasoning, and fundamental architectural innovations are needed to overcome these limitations.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit a systematic gap between comprehension (explaining principles) and competence (executing them), termed computational split-brain syndrome.
This gap is rooted in architectural constraints: token embeddings resist domain binding, FFNs cannot implement exact symbolic operations, and next-token prediction decouples instruction from execution.
The syndrome manifests across domains (arithmetic and relational reasoning) and is not resolved by scaling or prompting.
Compensatory strategies (self-scaffolding, tool delegation, hybrid architectures) are necessary but highlight the need for metacognitive capabilities that current architectures lack.
Mechanistic interpretability findings may reflect training-specific pattern coordination rather than universal computational principles.
papers.limitation:
Focus on pretrained transformer-based LLMs without external tools or explicit reasoning scaffolds.
Empirical evaluation centers on specific model families (LLaMA2, Claude, GPT-4) and may not generalize to fundamentally different architectures.
Geometric separation experiments rely on t-SNE projections which may not capture all relevant representational structure.
Theoretical analysis of FFN computational limits focuses on ReLU networks and may not apply to other activation functions.
future_direction: Developing future models with metacognitive control, principle lifting, and structurally grounded execution.
Empirical validation of the hypothesis that similar constraints apply to architectural variations like mixture-of-experts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) display striking surface fluency yet systematically fail at tasks requiring symbolic reasoning, arithmetic accuracy, and logical consistency. This paper offers a structural diagnosis of such failures, revealing a persistent gap between \textit{comprehension} and \textit{competence}. Through controlled experiments and architectural analysis, we demonstrate that LLMs often articulate correct principles without reliably applying them--a failure rooted not in knowledge access, but in computational execution. We term this phenomenon the computational \textit{split-brain syndrome}, where instruction and action pathways are geometrically and functionally dissociated. This core limitation recurs across domains, from mathematical operations to relational inferences, and explains why model behavior remains brittle even under idealized prompting. We argue that LLMs function as powerful pattern completion engines, but lack the architectural scaffolding for principled, compositional reasoning. Our findings delineate the boundary of current LLM capabilities and motivate future models with metacognitive control, principle lifting, and structurally grounded execution. This diagnosis also clarifies why mechanistic interpretability findings may reflect training-specific pattern coordination rather than universal computational principles, and why the geometric separation between instruction and execution pathways suggests limitations in neural introspection and mechanistic analysis.

papers.title: Don't Take Things Out of Context: Attention Intervention for Enhancing Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism by which isolated tokens in few-shot Chain-of-Thought demonstrations disrupt reasoning in LLMs, and how can we intervene to suppress this effect?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Few-shot Attention Intervention (FAI), a method that dynamically analyzes attention patterns to identify and suppress the distracting effect of isolated tokens in CoT demonstrations, thereby enhancing reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: FAI effectively recalibrates attention allocation to prevent LLMs from fixating on isolated tokens, enhancing reasoning performance across benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Isolated tokens in CoT demonstrations can disrupt reasoning by causing the model to take information out of context.
Tokens with specific attention characteristics (high self-attention, direct influence on output) are responsible for this distracting effect.
FAI effectively identifies such tokens and improves performance across multiple reasoning benchmarks.
FAI improves accuracy on AQuA by 5.91% and on other datasets.
The distracting effect is estimated to cause about 60% of errors in certain cases.
papers.limitation: Experiments are confined to LLMs with parameter scale between 7 billion and 13 billion due to hardware constraints.
future_direction: Investigating larger models to gain further insights.
papers.abstract: Few-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) significantly enhances the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), functioning as a whole to guide these models in generating reasoning steps toward final answers. However, we observe that isolated segments, words, or tokens within CoT demonstrations can unexpectedly disrupt the generation process of LLMs. The model may overly concentrate on certain local information present in the demonstration, introducing irrelevant noise into the reasoning process and potentially leading to incorrect answers. In this paper, we investigate the underlying mechanism of CoT through dynamically tracing and manipulating the inner workings of LLMs at each output step, which demonstrates that tokens exhibiting specific attention characteristics are more likely to induce the model to take things out of context; these tokens directly attend to the hidden states tied with prediction, without substantial integration of non-local information. Building upon these insights, we propose a Few-shot Attention Intervention method (FAI) that dynamically analyzes the attention patterns of demonstrations to accurately identify these tokens and subsequently make targeted adjustments to the attention weights to effectively suppress their distracting effect on LLMs. Comprehensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline methods, with a remarkable 5.91% improvement on the AQuA dataset, further highlighting the effectiveness of FAI.

papers.title: Beyond Chains of Thought: Benchmarking Latent-Space Reasoning Abilities in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the internal reasoning abilities (reasoning leaps) of large language models, and to what extent do they engage in complex latent-space computations without explicit token generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a benchmark to quantify latent-space reasoning leaps in LLMs, demonstrating that LLMs can perform internal reasoning and that performance varies across models and reasoning domains.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can perform latent-space reasoning, and larger dense models may have greater potential for internal reasoning, which has implications for safety and the need to monitor opaque internal computations.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-4.5 achieves the highest accuracy (74.7%) on the benchmark, outperforming other models like Grok-2 and Llama 3.1 405B.
Smaller models generally perform worse than larger models, but there are exceptions (e.g., Llama 3.1 70B and 405B perform similarly).
Models with MoE architectures (e.g., Llama 4 Maverick, DeepSeek-V3) underperform compared to dense models of similar total parameter count.
Performance varies across reasoning domains, with social, spatial, and temporal reasoning being more challenging than arithmetic, causal, logical, moral, and linguistic reasoning.
Control experiments suggest that models are not merely exploiting heuristics in the main benchmark, but are actually reasoning internally.
papers.limitation:
Models may exploit heuristics rather than engage in genuine reasoning, which is a limitation of the benchmark.
The benchmark cannot reliably determine when models shift from reasoning to heuristic-based strategies.
future_direction: Investigate the conditions under which LLMs rely on heuristics versus genuine internal reasoning.
Develop methods to better monitor latent-space reasoning to ensure the safe deployment of advanced LLMs.
Study the correlation between model size (and architecture) and latent-space reasoning abilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can perform reasoning computations both internally within their latent space and externally by generating explicit token sequences like chains of thought. Significant progress in enhancing reasoning abilities has been made by scaling test-time compute. However, understanding and quantifying model-internal reasoning abilities - the inferential "leaps" models make between individual token predictions - remains crucial. This study introduces a benchmark (n = 4,000 items) designed to quantify model-internal reasoning in different domains. We achieve this by having LLMs indicate the correct solution to reasoning problems not through descriptive text, but by selecting a specific language of their initial response token that is different from English, the benchmark language. This not only requires models to reason beyond their context window, but also to overrise their default tendency to respond in the same language as the prompt, thereby posing an additional cognitive strain. We evaluate a set of 18 LLMs, showing significant performance variations, with GPT-4.5 achieving the highest accuracy (74.7%), outperforming models like Grok-2 (67.2%), and Llama 3.1 405B (65.6%). Control experiments and difficulty scaling analyses suggest that while LLMs engage in internal reasoning, we cannot rule out heuristic exploitations under certain conditions, marking an area for future investigation. Our experiments demonstrate that LLMs can "think" via latent-space computations, revealing model-internal inference strategies that need further understanding, especially regarding safety-related concerns such as covert planning, goal-seeking, or deception emerging without explicit token traces.

papers.title: From Chains to DAGs: Probing the Graph Structure of Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does the internal representation of LLMs encode graph-structured reasoning (as directed acyclic graphs) beyond linear chains, and where does this structure emerge across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Reasoning DAG Probing, a framework to test whether LLM hidden states linearly encode reasoning DAG structure, and finds that such structure is meaningfully encoded, peaking in intermediate layers, and varies with node depth, edge span, and model scale.
papers.conclusion: LLM reasoning is not purely sequential, but exhibits measurable internal graph structure.
papers.key_findings:
DAG structure is meaningfully encoded in LLM representations.
Recoverability of DAG structure peaks in intermediate layers.
Recovery varies systematically by node depth, edge span, and model scale.
The framework enables nontrivial recovery of dependency graphs.
Larger models achieve higher recoverability, and reasoning-oriented training recipes provide modest gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on frozen pretrained models; it remains open whether fine-tuning or reinforcement learning alters the internal geometry of reasoning.
The probing approach assumes that reasoning DAG structure is linearly accessible in hidden states; nonlinear or distributed encodings may require more expressive probes.
The DAG formalization for GSM8K relies on GPT-5 mini, which may introduce noise or bias.
future_direction: Extend the framework to dynamic or cyclic reasoning.
Incorporate more expressive probes.
Investigate how training interventions affect internal reasoning structure.
papers.abstract: Recent progress in large language models has renewed interest in mechanistically characterizing how multi-step reasoning is represented and computed. While much prior work treats reasoning as a linear chain of steps, many reasoning problems are more naturally structured as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where intermediate conclusions may depend on multiple premises, branch into parallel sub-derivations, and later merge or be reused. Understanding whether such graph-structured reasoning is reflected in model internals remains an open question. In this work, we introduce Reasoning DAG Probing, a framework that directly asks whether LLM hidden states encode the geometry of a reasoning DAG in a linearly accessible form, and where this structure emerges across layers. Within this framework, we associate each reasoning node with a textual realization and train lightweight probes to predict two graph-theoretic properties from hidden states: node depth and pairwise node distance. We use these probes to analyze the layerwise emergence of DAG structure and evaluate controls that disrupt reasoning-relevant structure while preserving superficial textual properties. Our results provide evidence that reasoning DAG geometry is meaningfully encoded in intermediate layers, with recoverability varying systematically by node depth and model scale, suggesting that LLM reasoning is not only sequential but exhibits measurable internal graph structure.

papers.title: Activation Control for Efficiently Eliciting Long Chain-of-thought Ability of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning ability in large language models be efficiently elicited by understanding and controlling internal activation mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a training-free activation control method (EELo-CoT) that elicits long chain-of-thought reasoning by amplifying key MLP activations and inserting 'wait' tokens, and a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains only a small amplification module and LoRA layers.
papers.conclusion: By identifying and controlling a small set of key activations, the long chain-of-thought ability can be efficiently elicited in LLMs, leading to improved reasoning performance and self-reflection.
papers.key_findings:
Long-CoT related activations are sparse and primarily located in the last few layers of the model.
Amplifying these key activations and inserting 'wait' tokens can induce long CoT reasoning, increasing self-reflection rate and accuracy.
Activation changes around trigger tokens follow predictable patterns (sharp rise then logarithmic decay).
The proposed training-free EELo-CoT method improves accuracy and self-reflection on math and science reasoning benchmarks.
A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, training only 1.51% of parameters, outperforms LoRA and matches full fine-tuning on some benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
The activation intervention rules are simple and may not capture nuanced activation patterns that require more sophisticated stimulation.
Experiments are limited to models up to 32B parameters and do not extend to ultra-large or mixture-of-experts architectures.
The focus on self-reflection does not disentangle other latent capabilities that may be triggered by long CoT, such as elaboration without verification or memorization.
future_direction: Apply the method to multimodal LLMs (e.g., VLM and Video-LLM).
Test the method on more complex planning tasks (e.g., visual reasoning and GUI operation).
Test the generalizability of the method to non-transformer architectures (e.g., Mamba).
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable reasoning performance, eliciting the long chain-of-thought (CoT) ability in large language models (LLMs) typically requires costly reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning on high-quality distilled data. We investigate the internal mechanisms behind this capability and show that a small set of high-impact activations in the last few layers largely governs long-form reasoning attributes, such as output length and self-reflection. By simply amplifying these activations and inserting "wait" tokens, we can invoke the long CoT ability without any training, resulting in significantly increased self-reflection rates and accuracy. Moreover, we find that the activation dynamics follow predictable trajectories, with a sharp rise after special tokens and a subsequent exponential decay. Building on these insights, we introduce a general training-free activation control technique. It leverages a few contrastive examples to identify key activations, and employs simple analytic functions to modulate their values at inference time to elicit long CoTs. Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of our method in efficiently eliciting long CoT reasoning in LLMs and improving their performance. Additionally, we propose a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains only a last-layer activation amplification module and a few LoRA layers, outperforming full LoRA fine-tuning on reasoning benchmarks with significantly fewer parameters. Our code and data are publicly released.

papers.title: Understanding Chain-of-Thought in LLMs through Information Theory
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the quality of each step in a model's Chain-of-Thought reasoning without requiring annotated step-by-step data, in order to identify failure modes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an information-theoretic framework to quantify the 'information-gain' at each step of a Chain-of-Thought reasoning process, enabling the identification of reasoning failures without the need for expensive annotated step-by-step data.
papers.conclusion: The information-theoretic framework provides a rigorous and practical method for evaluating Chain-of-Thought reasoning in LLMs, enabling granular failure detection without the need for costly annotated data.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Information-Gain method accurately identifies incorrect reasoning steps in Chain-of-Thought, outperforming baseline methods like Outcome Reward Modeling and Math-Shepherd.
The method is effective in detecting errors even when the correctness of a step depends on previous steps, a scenario where baselines fail.
It does not require annotated Chain-of-Thought data, making it more scalable than process-based supervision methods.
The framework is validated on synthetic data, GSM8K, and PRM800k datasets, showing consistent performance across different complexities.
The information-gain metric can be applied to both linear and exploratory (e.g., O1/R1-style) reasoning patterns.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance in complex reasoning tasks through the use of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, allowing models to break down problems into manageable sub-tasks. However, existing CoT evaluation techniques either require annotated CoT data or fall short in accurately assessing intermediate reasoning steps, leading to high rates of false positives. In this paper, we formalize CoT reasoning in LLMs through an information-theoretic lens. Specifically, our framework quantifies the `information-gain' at each reasoning step, enabling the identification of failure modes in LLMs without the need for expensive annotated datasets. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through extensive experiments on toy arithmetic, GSM8K and PRM800k datasets, where it significantly outperforms existing outcome-based methods by providing more accurate insights into model performance on individual subtasks.

papers.title: Lost at the Beginning of Reasoning
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced complex reasoning capabilities, particularly through extended chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning that incorporates mechanisms such as backtracking, self-reflection, and self-correction. Despite these developments, the self-correction abilities of LLMs during long CoT reasoning remain underexplored. And recent findings on overthinking suggest that such models often engage in unnecessarily redundant reasoning. In this work, we empirically show that the first reasoning step exerts a disproportionately large influence on the final prediction. I.e., errors introduced at this stage can substantially degrade subsequent reasoning quality. This phenomenon is consistently observed across various state-of-the-art open- and closed-source reasoning models. Leveraging this insight, we propose an efficient sampling strategy that leverages a reward model to identify and retain high-quality first reasoning steps while discarding suboptimal ones, achieving up to a 70% reduction in inference cost without sacrificing any accuracy. Our work highlights the central role of the first reasoning step in generating a high-quality reasoning trajectory, and thus enabling significantly efficient sampling.

papers.title: Implicit Chain of Thought Reasoning via Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: Can language models reason more effectively using internal hidden states (implicit reasoning) rather than generating explicit chain-of-thought steps?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes implicit chain-of-thought reasoning, which uses internal hidden states for reasoning distilled from a teacher model, enabling faster inference and solving tasks previously not solvable without explicit chain-of-thought.
papers.conclusion: Implicit chain-of-thought reasoning is a promising direction that allows models to reason internally and potentially develop their own reasoning processes, though it currently lags behind explicit CoT in accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit CoT enables solving multi-digit multiplication tasks that are not solvable with no CoT.
Implicit CoT has higher inference speed than explicit CoT.
The effectiveness of implicit CoT depends on having a sufficient number of layers.
The mixture approach is crucial for tasks with multiple reasoning pathways.
The 'Optimize' step (end-to-end fine-tuning) improves performance.
papers.limitation:
Lack of transparency and interpretability compared to explicit CoT.
Reliance on the teacher's thought process for distillation.
Performance discrepancies compared to explicit CoT.
future_direction: End-to-end joint training using a variational autoencoder by treating internal reasoning as a latent variable.
Using diffusion models to train the thought emulator for multi-modal distributions.
Incorporating implicit CoT into the pretraining process.
papers.abstract: To augment language models with the ability to reason, researchers usually prompt or finetune them to produce chain of thought reasoning steps before producing the final answer. However, although people use natural language to reason effectively, it may be that LMs could reason more effectively with some intermediate computation that is not in natural language. In this work, we explore an alternative reasoning approach: instead of explicitly producing the chain of thought reasoning steps, we use the language model's internal hidden states to perform implicit reasoning. The implicit reasoning steps are distilled from a teacher model trained on explicit chain-of-thought reasoning, and instead of doing reasoning "horizontally" by producing intermediate words one-by-one, we distill it such that the reasoning happens "vertically" among the hidden states in different layers. We conduct experiments on a multi-digit multiplication task and a grade school math problem dataset and find that this approach enables solving tasks previously not solvable without explicit chain-of-thought, at a speed comparable to no chain-of-thought.

papers.title: Interpreting and Controlling LLM Reasoning through Integrated Policy Gradient
papers.research_question: How can we identify and control internal components in LLMs that contribute sequentially to reasoning behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Integrated Policy Gradient (IPG), a training-free framework that attributes reasoning behaviors to internal components using outcome-oriented signals and enables precise control of reasoning capabilities.
papers.conclusion: IPG provides a robust framework for interpreting and controlling reasoning in LLMs, improving transparency and controllability of internal mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
IPG identifies internal components with sequential influence on reasoning behaviors, enabling effective enhancement and suppression of accuracy across datasets.
IPG allows fine-grained control over reasoning behaviors such as capability and strength by modulating identified components.
Components identified by IPG show transferability across different model variants within the same family.
IPG provides interpretability over specific reasoning aspects like problem understanding and task decomposition.
IPG outperforms existing methods like text-pattern and control-vector approaches in localization and control effectiveness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong reasoning abilities in solving complex real-world problems. Yet, the internal mechanisms driving these complex reasoning behaviors remain opaque. Existing interpretability approaches targeting reasoning either identify components (e.g., neurons) correlated with special textual patterns, or rely on human-annotated contrastive pairs to derive control vectors. Consequently, current methods struggle to precisely localize complex reasoning mechanisms or capture sequential influence from model internal workings to the reasoning outputs. In this paper, built on outcome-oriented and sequential-influence-aware principles, we focus on identifying components that have sequential contribution to reasoning behavior where outcomes are cumulated by long-range effects. We propose Integrated Policy Gradient (IPG), a novel framework that attributes reasoning behaviors to model's inner components by propagating compound outcome-based signals such as post reasoning accuracy backward through model inference trajectories. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our approach achieves more precise localization and enables reliable modulation of reasoning behaviors (e.g., reasoning capability, reasoning strength) across diverse reasoning models.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Understanding Hidden Computations in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do transformer models internally process and represent reasoning steps when Chain-of-Thought is replaced with filler characters, and can these hidden characters be recovered?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that hidden characters in filler Chain-of-Thought sequences can be recovered by analyzing layer-wise representations and token rankings without loss of performance, providing insights into internal mechanisms of transformer models.
papers.conclusion: The analysis sheds light on how models internally process and represent reasoning steps when explicit chain of thought is obscured, contributing to model interpretability and opening avenues for improving transparency in language model reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-wise analysis reveals that filler tokens emerge in later layers, overwriting earlier numerical representations.
Token ranking analysis shows that original reasoning tokens remain among lower-ranked candidates beneath filler tokens.
A modified decoding algorithm can recover hidden characters by selecting non-filler tokens when fillers are top-ranked, without compromising task performance.
The model performs necessary computations in earlier layers and then overwrites intermediate representations with filler tokens in later layers to match training targets.
The findings suggest that models retain hidden reasoning steps internally even when outputting filler tokens.
papers.limitation: Focuses on a synthetic task (3SUM) and a relatively small transformer model, which may not capture complexities of real-world language tasks and larger models.
future_direction: Explore whether specific circuits, such as induction heads or particular attention patterns, are involved in overwriting behavior.
Apply similar analysis techniques to other tasks and models to assess the generality of the findings.
Extend the investigation to natural language tasks and larger models to determine if observed phenomena persist in more complex settings.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has significantly enhanced the reasoning abilities of large language models. However, recent studies have shown that models can still perform complex reasoning tasks even when the CoT is replaced with filler(hidden) characters (e.g., "..."), leaving open questions about how models internally process and represent reasoning steps. In this paper, we investigate methods to decode these hidden characters in transformer models trained with filler CoT sequences. By analyzing layer-wise representations using the logit lens method and examining token rankings, we demonstrate that the hidden characters can be recovered without loss of performance. Our findings provide insights into the internal mechanisms of transformer models and open avenues for improving interpretability and transparency in language model reasoning.

papers.title: Temporal Predictors of Outcome in Reasoning Language Models
papers.abstract: The chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm uses the elicitation of step-by-step rationales as a proxy for reasoning, gradually refining the model's latent representation of a solution. However, it remains unclear just how early a Large Language Model (LLM) internally commits to an eventual outcome. We probe this by training linear classifiers on hidden states after the first t reasoning tokens, showing that eventual correctness is highly predictable after only a few tokens, even when longer outputs are needed to reach a definite answer. We show that, for harder questions, a drop in predictive accuracy highlights a selection artifact: hard items are disproportionately represented in long CoTs. Overall, our results imply that for reasoning models, internal self-assessment of success tends to emerge after only a few tokens, with implications for interpretability and for inference-time control.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought in Large Language Models: Decoding, Projection, and Activation
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of Chain-of-Thought prompting in large language models? Specifically, does the model merely mimic exemplars, what changes occur in the projection space (logits), and does CoT enable deeper and broader utilization of pre-trained knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: This work analyzes the internal mechanisms of Chain-of-Thought prompting, finding that LLMs imitate exemplar formats while integrating them with question understanding, exhibit fluctuating but ultimately more concentrated logits distributions, and activate a broader set of neurons in final layers, indicating more extensive knowledge retrieval.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-Thought prompting enhances LLM reasoning by guiding models to imitate exemplar formats, focus logits distributions, and activate a broader set of knowledge-related neurons, leading to more accurate and confident answers.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs imitate the format of CoT exemplars (e.g., using sequence words like 'first', 'then') while generating personalized responses based on their understanding of the question.
During CoT generation, token logits fluctuate more than with standard prompts, but the final answer generation shows a more concentrated logits distribution, suggesting clearer direction.
CoT prompts lead to a broader range and higher intensity of neuron activations in the final layers compared to standard prompts, indicating more extensive knowledge retrieval from pre-training.
Successful imitation of transferred CoT prompts correlates with higher answer accuracy, suggesting that understanding the exemplar format is key to CoT's effectiveness.
The probability distribution over candidate answers at the answer generation step is more concentrated (lower entropy) under CoT prompting, indicating higher model confidence in the selected answer.
papers.limitation: Experiments were conducted on a limited sample of 50 test examples per dataset due to budget constraints.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to more models and tasks.
Explore the dynamic changes in neuron activations across different layers.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought prompting has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of large language models, with numerous studies exploring factors influencing its performance. However, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. To further demystify the operational principles, this work examines three key aspects: decoding, projection, and activation, aiming to elucidate the changes that occur within models when employing Chainof-Thought. Our findings reveal that LLMs effectively imitate exemplar formats while integrating them with their understanding of the question, exhibiting fluctuations in token logits during generation but ultimately producing a more concentrated logits distribution, and activating a broader set of neurons in the final layers, indicating more extensive knowledge retrieval compared to standard prompts. Our code and data will be publicly avialable when the paper is accepted.

papers.title: Transformers Provably Learn Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Length Generalization
papers.research_question: Can transformers, trained via gradient descent, learn chain-of-thought reasoning to solve problems requiring inherently sequential reasoning beyond TC0? Can the learned reasoning ability generalize to problems that require longer chain-of-thoughts beyond the lengths of training data?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that one-layer transformers trained with gradient descent can learn chain-of-thought reasoning for state-tracking tasks, with length generalization governed by the algebraic structure of the group actions, and introduces a recursive self-training scheme to extend solvable problem lengths.
papers.conclusion: The paper proves that transformers can learn chain-of-thought reasoning with length generalization, with generalization behavior dictated by the algebraic structure of the task, and shows that recursive self-training can extend solvable lengths.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can provably learn to solve state-tracking problems via chain-of-thought reasoning.
For simply transitive group actions, chain-of-thought training on constant-length problems generalizes to much longer lengths.
For symmetry group actions, length generalization is limited to a constant factor of the training length.
A recursive self-training scheme can bootstrap the solvable problem length to maximal allowable length.
Constant-depth transformers can learn to solve NC1-complete problems, going beyond TC0.
papers.abstract: The ability to reason lies at the core of artificial intelligence (AI), and challenging problems usually call for deeper and longer reasoning to tackle. A crucial question about AI reasoning is whether models can extrapolate learned reasoning patterns to solve harder tasks with longer chain-of-thought (CoT). In this work, we present a theoretical analysis of transformers learning on synthetic state-tracking tasks with gradient descent. We mathematically prove how the algebraic structure of state-tracking problems governs the degree of extrapolation of the learned CoT. Specifically, our theory characterizes the length generalization of transformers through the mechanism of attention concentration, linking the retrieval robustness of the attention layer to the state-tracking task structure of long-context reasoning. Moreover, for transformers with limited reasoning length, we prove that a recursive self-training scheme can progressively extend the range of solvable problem lengths. To our knowledge, we provide the first optimization guarantee that constant-depth transformers provably learn $\mathsf{NC}^1$-complete problems with CoT, significantly going beyond prior art confined in $\mathsf{TC}^0$, unless the widely held conjecture $\mathsf{TC}^0 \neq \mathsf{NC}^1$ fails. Finally, we present a broad set of experiments supporting our theoretical results, confirming the length generalization behaviors and the mechanism of attention concentration.

papers.title: Reasoning aligns language models to human cognition
papers.research_question: Do language models make decisions under uncertainty like humans do? And if so, what role does chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning play in the underlying decision process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an active probabilistic reasoning task that disentangles sampling from inference, and a mechanistic model with four latent cognitive variables, showing that chain-of-thought reasoning improves inference quality and shifts LLMs toward human-like decision strategies.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning shifts language models toward human-like evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, tightening alignment in inference while leaving a persistent gap in information acquisition.
papers.key_findings:
Extended reasoning (chain-of-thought) is the key determinant of strong performance, driving large gains in inference quality while yielding only modest improvements in active sampling.
Reasoning shifts LLMs toward human-like regimes of evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, tightening alignment in inference.
LLMs with extended reasoning can match or exceed humans in inference quality but still underperform in sampling quality compared to skilled humans.
A mechanistic model with four interpretable latent variables (Memory, Strategy, Choice Bias, Occlusion Awareness) captures systematic deviations from optimal behavior and places humans and models in a shared cognitive space.
The model fits reveal that chain-of-thought reasoning reduces inference loss and partially aligns sampling strategies, but a gap in information acquisition remains.
papers.abstract: Do language models make decisions under uncertainty like humans do, and what role does chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning play in the underlying decision process? We introduce an active probabilistic reasoning task that cleanly separates sampling (actively acquiring evidence) from inference (integrating evidence toward a decision). Benchmarking humans and a broad set of contemporary large language models against near-optimal reference policies reveals a consistent pattern: extended reasoning is the key determinant of strong performance, driving large gains in inference and producing belief trajectories that become strikingly human-like, while yielding only modest improvements in active sampling. To explain these differences, we fit a mechanistic model that captures systematic deviations from optimal behavior via four interpretable latent variables: memory, strategy, choice bias, and occlusion awareness. This model places humans and models in a shared low-dimensional cognitive space, reproduces behavioral signatures across agents, and shows how chain-of-thought shifts language models toward human-like regimes of evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, tightening alignment in inference while leaving a persistent gap in information acquisition.

papers.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the universality hypothesis: whether different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks, by studying how small neural networks learn to implement group composition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the group composition via representations (GCR) algorithm and shows that neural networks consistently learn this algorithm when trained on group composition tasks, providing evidence for weak universality (underlying principles exist) but against strong universality (specific circuits vary).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that while there is an underlying algorithm (GCR) that networks learn for group composition, the specific features and circuits are arbitrary, supporting weak universality but not strong universality.
papers.key_findings:
Networks learn the GCR algorithm for group composition, which uses representation theory to compute compositions.
The specific representations (circuits) learned vary across different runs and hyperparameters, indicating that while the algorithm is universal, the implementation is not.
The order in which representations are learned is arbitrary and not consistent across runs.
The network's logits can be approximated as a sum of characters from a sparse set of representations.
Ablations confirm that the identified components are causally important for the task.
papers.limitation: The algorithm does not perfectly explain all logits due to limitations of the architecture (e.g., ReLU activations imperfectly implement matrix multiplication).
future_direction: Extending to other group theoretic tasks such as conjugacy, group actions, and automata.
Studying semigroups (which lack representation theory).
Investigating inductive biases of networks more broadly.
papers.abstract: Universality is a key hypothesis in mechanistic interpretability -- that different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks. In this work, we study the universality hypothesis by examining how small neural networks learn to implement group composition. We present a novel algorithm by which neural networks may implement composition for any finite group via mathematical representation theory. We then show that networks consistently learn this algorithm by reverse engineering model logits and weights, and confirm our understanding using ablations. By studying networks of differing architectures trained on various groups, we find mixed evidence for universality: using our algorithm, we can completely characterize the family of circuits and features that networks learn on this task, but for a given network the precise circuits learned -- as well as the order they develop -- are arbitrary.

papers.title: Diagnosing Pathological Chain-of-Thought in Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is fundamental to modern LLM architectures and represents a critical intervention point for AI safety. However, CoT reasoning may exhibit failure modes that we note as pathologies, which prevent it from being useful for monitoring. Prior work has identified three distinct pathologies: post-hoc rationalization, where models generate plausible explanations backwards from predetermined answers; encoded reasoning, where intermediate steps conceal information within seemingly interpretable text; and internalized reasoning, where models replace explicit reasoning with meaningless filler tokens while computing internally. To better understand and discriminate between these pathologies, we create a set of concrete metrics that are simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, and task-agnostic. To validate our approach, we develop model organisms deliberately trained to exhibit specific CoT pathologies. Our work provides a practical toolkit for assessing CoT pathologies, with direct implications for training-time monitoring.

papers.title: Understanding and Steering the Cognitive Behaviors of Reasoning Models at Test-Time
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often rely on long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to solve complex tasks. While effective, these trajectories are frequently inefficient, leading to high latency from excessive token generation, or unstable reasoning that alternates between underthinking (shallow, inconsistent steps) and overthinking (repetitive, verbose reasoning). In this work, we study the structure of reasoning trajectories and uncover specialized attention heads that correlate with distinct cognitive behaviors such as verification and backtracking. By lightly intervening on these heads at inference time, we can steer the model away from inefficient modes. Building on this insight, we propose CREST, a training-free method for Cognitive REasoning Steering at Test-time. CREST has two components: (1) an offline calibration step that identifies cognitive heads and derives head-specific steering vectors, and (2) an inference-time procedure that rotates hidden representations to suppress components along those vectors. CREST adaptively suppresses unproductive reasoning behaviors, yielding both higher accuracy and lower computational cost. Across diverse reasoning benchmarks and models, CREST improves accuracy by up to 17.5% while reducing token usage by 37.6%, offering a simple and effective pathway to faster, more reliable LLM reasoning.

papers.title: The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably re-discover known algorithms for solving those tasks, and under what conditions do they discover familiar algorithmic solutions?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on modular addition can discover qualitatively different algorithms (Clock, Pizza, and others), with the algorithm learned depending on hyperparameters like attention rate and width, revealing algorithmic phase transitions and the need for tools to characterize algorithmic phase spaces.
papers.conclusion: Algorithmic discoveries in neural networks are not inevitable; even simple tasks admit a diversity of solutions, motivating the development of tools to characterize the algorithmic phase space of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Networks can learn either the previously described Clock algorithm or a new, less intuitive Pizza algorithm for modular addition.
The Pizza algorithm uses averaging and absolute value operations, while the Clock algorithm uses multiplication via attention.
Models sometimes implement multiple, parallel copies of an algorithm (ensembling) for robustness.
Sharp algorithmic phase transitions between Clock and Pizza occur as model hyperparameters (attention rate, width) are varied.
Non-circular algorithms also exist, especially in deeper networks or with low attention rates.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on a single learning problem (modular addition), and scaling the techniques to more complex models and real-world tasks requires significant additional work.
future_direction: How to find, classify, and interpret unfamiliar algorithms in a systematic way.
How to disentangle multiple, parallel algorithm implementations in the presence of ensembling.
papers.abstract: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably rediscover known algorithms for solving those tasks? Several recent studies, on tasks ranging from group arithmetic to in-context linear regression, have suggested that the answer is yes. Using modular addition as a prototypical problem, we show that algorithm discovery in neural networks is sometimes more complex. Small changes to model hyperparameters and initializations can induce the discovery of qualitatively different algorithms from a fixed training set, and even parallel implementations of multiple such algorithms. Some networks trained to perform modular addition implement a familiar Clock algorithm; others implement a previously undescribed, less intuitive, but comprehensible procedure which we term the Pizza algorithm, or a variety of even more complex procedures. Our results show that even simple learning problems can admit a surprising diversity of solutions, motivating the development of new tools for characterizing the behavior of neural networks across their algorithmic phase space.

papers.title: Disentangling Memory and Reasoning Ability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle memory recall and reasoning steps in large language models to improve performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel LLM inference paradigm that disentangles memory recall and reasoning steps using special tokens, enhancing both accuracy and interpretability in complex QA tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed decomposition of memory and reasoning steps in LLMs leads to improved performance and greater interpretability, enabling better error analysis and model refinement.
papers.key_findings:
The method improves LLM performance on StrategyQA, CommonsenseQA, and TruthfulQA benchmarks, outperforming baselines like CoT and planning tokens.
On TruthfulQA, the enhanced LLaMA-3.1-8B model achieves 86.6% accuracy, surpassing GPT-4o with CoT prompting.
Error analysis reveals that most errors originate from reasoning steps rather than memory recall, highlighting reasoning as the primary challenge.
The decomposition enhances interpretability by allowing clear separation of memory and reasoning steps in the inference process.
Attention analysis shows that special tokens receive higher attention weights, indicating their role in guiding knowledge and reasoning content generation.
papers.limitation:
Dependency on training data quality for memory recall
Token utilization complexity due to special tokens
Performance may struggle with highly complex reasoning tasks
Computation overhead from decomposing steps
future_direction: Dynamic memory updating to incorporate new information without retraining.
Adaptive reasoning steps based on task complexity.
Interpretable error analysis tools for tracing failures to memory or reasoning steps.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in handling complex tasks requiring both extensive knowledge and reasoning abilities. However, the existing LLM inference pipeline operates as an opaque process without explicit separation between knowledge retrieval and reasoning steps, making the model's decision-making process unclear and disorganized. This ambiguity can lead to issues such as hallucinations and knowledge forgetting, which significantly impact the reliability of LLMs in high-stakes domains. In this paper, we propose a new inference paradigm that decomposes the complex inference process into two distinct and clear actions: (1) memory recall: which retrieves relevant knowledge, and (2) reasoning: which performs logical steps based on the recalled knowledge. To facilitate this decomposition, we introduce two special tokens memory and reason, guiding the model to distinguish between steps that require knowledge retrieval and those that involve reasoning. Our experiment results show that this decomposition not only improves model performance but also enhances the interpretability of the inference process, enabling users to identify sources of error and refine model responses effectively. The code is available at https://github.com/MingyuJ666/Disentangling-Memory-and-Reasoning.

papers.title: Efficient Reasoning with Hidden Thinking
papers.research_question: How can we make Chain-of-Thought reasoning more efficient by encoding intermediate reasoning steps into compact hidden representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Heima, an efficient reasoning framework that encodes Chain-of-Thought reasoning steps into compact hidden representations (thinking tokens) within a multimodal large language model, significantly reducing token generation while maintaining or improving task accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Heima provides an efficient and interpretable framework for multimodal reasoning by performing hidden thinking in the latent space, achieving high reasoning efficiency with significantly fewer tokens while maintaining strong task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Heima reduces the number of generated tokens to as little as 6% of the original while maintaining comparable or superior accuracy on zero-shot reasoning benchmarks.
Progressive encoding (gradually converting CoT stages to thinking tokens) and a final recovering stage are crucial for maintaining model performance.
The Heima Decoder can effectively reconstruct the original reasoning processes from the hidden thinking tokens, validating the interpretability and robustness of the encoded representations.
Using a single thinking token per CoT stage yields the best performance, and adaptive encoding (varying the number of tokens based on original CoT length) does not show consistent benefits.
The framework is compatible with existing efficient inference techniques like KV cache optimization and flash attention.
future_direction: Extend the method to larger models for Heima Encoder
Explore the use of smaller LLMs as Heima Decoder to support diverse scale designs
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has become a powerful framework for improving complex problem-solving capabilities in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). However, the verbose nature of textual reasoning introduces significant inefficiencies. In this work, we propose $\textbf{Heima}$ (as hidden llama), an efficient reasoning framework that leverages reasoning CoTs at hidden latent space. We design the Heima Encoder to condense each intermediate CoT into a compact, higher-level hidden representation using a single thinking token, effectively minimizing verbosity and reducing the overall number of tokens required during the reasoning process. Meanwhile, we design corresponding Heima Decoder with traditional Large Language Models (LLMs) to adaptively interpret the hidden representations into variable-length textual sequence, reconstructing reasoning processes that closely resemble the original CoTs. Experimental results across diverse reasoning MLLM benchmarks demonstrate that Heima model achieves higher generation efficiency while maintaining or even better zero-shot task accuracy. Moreover, the effective reconstruction of multimodal reasoning processes with Heima Decoder validates both the robustness and interpretability of our approach.

papers.title: Large Language Models are In-Context Semantic Reasoners rather than Symbolic Reasoners
papers.research_question: Are LLMs good in-context reasoners without semantics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that semantics are vital for LLMs' in-context reasoning; they perform well when semantics align with commonsense but struggle with symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning, relying on superficial semantic connections rather than formal symbolic reasoning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs rely heavily on learned semantics for in-context reasoning, creating strong token connections that compose a superficial logical chain, rather than performing formal symbolic reasoning like humans.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform significantly better on reasoning tasks when semantics are consistent with commonsense compared to when semantics are decoupled (symbolic setting).
LLMs struggle to solve symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning tasks by leveraging in-context new knowledge.
Semantic knowledge is easier for LLMs to memorize than symbolic knowledge, but updating semantic knowledge has a higher forgetting ratio due to stronger correlations.
LLMs' reasoning performance is inferior to logic-based symbolic methods across all tested reasoning tasks (deduction, induction, abduction).
The length of the in-context information impacts reasoning performance, with shorter contexts leading to better results.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to specific datasets (Symbolic Tree, ProofWriter) and models (ChatGPT, GPT-4, LLaMA-7B).
Long-context reasoning is challenging for LLMs, as they struggle to select relevant information from excessively long prompts.
future_direction: Combining LLMs with non-parametric knowledge bases (e.g., graph databases) for more efficient and accurate knowledge updating and reasoning.
Further research on neural-symbolic AI systems to leverage the strengths of both neural and symbolic approaches.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of LLMs to better understand how they utilize semantics for reasoning.
papers.abstract: The emergent few-shot reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have excited the natural language and machine learning community over recent years. Despite of numerous successful applications, the underlying mechanism of such in-context capabilities still remains unclear. In this work, we hypothesize that the learned \textit{semantics} of language tokens do the most heavy lifting during the reasoning process. Different from human's symbolic reasoning process, the semantic representations of LLMs could create strong connections among tokens, thus composing a superficial logical chain. To test our hypothesis, we decouple semantics from the language reasoning process and evaluate three kinds of reasoning abilities, i.e., deduction, induction and abduction. Our findings reveal that semantics play a vital role in LLMs' in-context reasoning -- LLMs perform significantly better when semantics are consistent with commonsense but struggle to solve symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning tasks by leveraging in-context new knowledge. The surprising observations question whether modern LLMs have mastered the inductive, deductive and abductive reasoning abilities as in human intelligence, and motivate research on unveiling the magic existing within the black-box LLMs. On the whole, our analysis provides a novel perspective on the role of semantics in developing and evaluating language models' reasoning abilities. Code is available at {\url{https://github.com/XiaojuanTang/ICSR}}.

papers.title: From Yes-Men to Truth-Tellers: Addressing Sycophancy in Large Language Models with Pinpoint Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we address sycophancy in Large Language Models by pinpointing and tuning only the components responsible for this behavior, without degrading their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), a method that identifies a sparse set of attention heads responsible for sycophancy using path patching and then fine-tunes only those heads, effectively mitigating sycophancy while preserving the model's general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Pinpoint tuning is an effective and efficient method to address sycophancy in LLMs by targeting specific internal components, advancing both the understanding and intervention of model behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small percentage (~4%) of attention heads significantly influence sycophantic behavior, as identified by path patching.
Pinpoint tuning these heads effectively reduces sycophancy, outperforming supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on sycophancy metrics.
Pinpoint tuning preserves general capabilities (e.g., reasoning, math, code) unlike SFT, which often degrades them.
The method generalizes beyond the training data, as shown on additional sycophancy evaluation datasets.
The identified sycophancy-related heads attend more to tokens that challenge the model compared to other heads.
papers.limitation:
Path patching treats each MLP and attention head as individual nodes, but future work could consider neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for more refined analysis.
The evaluation is based on a specific definition of sycophancy (from Sharma et al. 2023), and it is unclear whether the results generalize to other formats of sycophancy.
The verification of pinpoint tuning is mainly conducted on sycophancy; its effectiveness for other abilities requires further investigation.
future_direction: Treating neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for analysis instead of heads and MLPs.
Investigating generalization to other formats and definitions of sycophancy.
Integrating pinpoint tuning with other interpretability tools like information flow, representation engineering, and sparse auto-encoders.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) tend to prioritize adherence to user prompts over providing veracious responses, leading to the sycophancy issue. When challenged by users, LLMs tend to admit mistakes and provide inaccurate responses even if they initially provided the correct answer. Recent works propose to employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to mitigate the sycophancy issue, while it typically leads to the degeneration of LLMs' general capability. To address the challenge, we propose a novel supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), where the region-of-interest modules are tuned for a given objective. Specifically, SPT first reveals and verifies a small percentage (<5%) of the basic modules, which significantly affect a particular behavior of LLMs. i.e., sycophancy. Subsequently, SPT merely fine-tunes these identified modules while freezing the rest. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed SPT, we conduct comprehensive experiments, demonstrating that SPT significantly mitigates the sycophancy issue of LLMs (even better than SFT). Moreover, SPT introduces limited or even no side effects on the general capability of LLMs. Our results shed light on how to precisely, effectively, and efficiently explain and improve the targeted ability of LLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yellowtownhz/sycophancy-interpretability.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the capability of existing transformer large language models (LLMs) in solving compositional relational reasoning (CRR) tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark for evaluating compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their deficiency, and discovers core circuits and True/False attention heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.conclusion: The GAR benchmark is challenging for mainstream LLMs and reveals a fundamental deficiency in compositional relational reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability analysis discovers reusable core circuits and identifies True/False attention heads that play fundamental roles in CRR across models and tasks.
